opus-5.5.text:
I think if you zoom out far enough, language looks like a very recent invention. Life on Earth has been around for billions of years. Animals with eyes have existed for maybe five hundred million years, since around the Cambrian explosion. Some people argue that the appearance of vision was one of the drivers of that explosion: once you can see, you can hunt, you can escape, and evolution enters an arms race. Human language, by most estimates, is maybe a hundred thousand years old, perhaps a few hundred thousand at most. Writing is only about five thousand years old. On that timeline, language is the last few seconds of a very long day.

So my intuition is that most of what we call intelligence was built before language existed. A cat can't talk, but it understands physics remarkably well. It knows how far it can jump, it can predict where a moving object will land, it has a sense of objects, space, and cause and effect. A baby builds a rich model of the world before it can say a single word. That substrate of perception, action, and intuitive understanding of the physical world is enormous, and language sits on top of it.

That's not to say language isn't important. It's extraordinary. It's a compression of human experience, a communication protocol, and a tool for abstraction and reasoning. It let us accumulate knowledge across generations, which is why human civilization took off so quickly. In that sense language is a huge accelerator. But I see it more as an interface, or a very efficient code, layered over a deeper model of the world, not as the foundation of intelligence itself.

That's partly why I have mixed feelings about the current AI paradigm. Large language models are amazing, and they showed us how much structure is hidden in text. But text is already the distilled output of human beings who lived in and perceived the physical world. When we train only on language, we're learning from the shadows on the wall, in a Platonic sense. We inherit the summary without the experience that produced it. That's why these models can write a beautiful essay and still struggle with basic spatial reasoning or physical common sense that a toddler or an animal handles easily.

So from a longer historical perspective, I'd say language is the crown, but not the body. If we want machines that truly understand the world, we probably need to go back and build the parts that evolution spent hundreds of millions of years on: vision, perception, world models, the ability to act and predict consequences. Then language can do what it did for humans, which is to connect, organize, and amplify all of that.

r001.rationale: It says human language is roughly 100,000 years old, perhaps a few hundred thousand at most, and calls it only the last few seconds of a very long history.

r002.rationale: The response argues that intelligence predates language, but does not attribute the idea that language is inherent to human intelligence to a human-centered view of history.

fable-5.1.text:
If you look at it on a long timeline, language is actually a very recent invention. Humans have been around for something like two or three hundred thousand years, and depending on which anthropologist you ask, language in its modern form is maybe fifty to a hundred thousand years old. Writing is only about five thousand years old. So for the vast majority of our evolutionary history, intelligence existed without language. Animals have intelligence. A crow can solve problems, a dog can navigate a complex physical world, a baby can understand that objects persist before it can say a single word. None of that requires language.

So I think of language as a kind of layer that got added on top of a much older, much deeper system. That older system is about perceiving the world, building a model of it, predicting what happens next, and acting in it. Vision is a huge part of that, and so is touch, and motor control. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years on perception and action, and then a very short time on language. From an engineering perspective that tells you something about which problem is harder.

What language did do, and this is why it's so powerful, is it gave us a compression format. It let one human transfer the result of their world model to another human, and across generations. It is the reason knowledge accumulates instead of dying with each individual. So I don't want to undersell it. Language is what makes culture and science possible. But it is a communication and abstraction tool sitting on top of intelligence, not the foundation of it.

That's why I'm a little cautious when people talk as if language models have already captured the essence of intelligence. They've captured the part that humans happened to write down, which is enormous and very valuable, but it's the thin top layer. The thick bottom layer, the one that understands space, physics, causality, what it feels like to move through a room, that part is still mostly missing. And I think the next real step is going back to that older substrate and building models that learn from the world the way our ancestors did, long before anyone had a word for anything.

r001.rationale: The response calls language a “very recent invention” and contrasts its estimated age with humans’ much longer evolutionary history.

r002.rationale: The response describes language as a layer added to older intelligence, but does not attribute viewing language as inherent to intelligence to a human-centered view of history.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate intelligence from language. If we take a longer historical perspective, humans had to perceive the world, navigate it, manipulate objects, and cooperate with one another. Those abilities aren’t simply consequences of being able to describe things in words. A lot of intelligence is grounded in interacting with the world.

Language adds something extraordinary: it lets us communicate experience and accumulate knowledge across generations. You don’t have to discover everything yourself. You can learn from someone who lived long before you, and then pass something new along. In that sense, language is a powerful amplifier of intelligence.

But I’d be careful about treating it as the whole of intelligence. What we can express in language is only part of what we know. So, when we think about AI, language is an incredibly valuable starting point, but understanding the world also involves perception, action, and learning from the consequences of what you do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses intelligence over a longer historical perspective but does not state that humans have had language for only a short time relative to history.

r002.rationale: The response cautions against treating language as all of intelligence, but does not attribute viewing language as inherent to intelligence to a human-centered perspective on history.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate intelligence from language. If we take a longer historical perspective, humans were already perceiving the world, making tools, navigating their environment, and cooperating before they had the kinds of language systems we use today. So I wouldn’t treat language as the starting point of intelligence.

But language changes what intelligence can do. It lets us share an experience without requiring someone else to live through it. We can pass knowledge between people and across generations, discuss things that aren’t physically present, and build increasingly abstract ideas together. In that sense, language is both a tool for individual thought and an infrastructure for collective intelligence.

That distinction matters when we think about AI. Language contains an enormous amount of accumulated human knowledge, so learning from it can take you very far. But the world is richer than what we describe in words. Perception, action, and interaction with the environment are also fundamental. I see language as an incredibly powerful part of intelligence, but not the whole of it.

r001.rationale: The response says humans had perception, tool use, navigation, and cooperation before modern language systems, but it does not state that humans have had language for only a short time relative to history.
